title: End of the 2026 respiratory syncytial virus season - NICD

analysis.time: The 2026 RSV season ended in week 34 (week starting 17 August 2026). The season began in week 11 (week starting 9 March 2026) and peaked in week 25 (week starting 15 June 2026).
analysis.location_and_population: The event occurred in South Africa, specifically among children aged <5 years enrolled in inpatient pneumonia surveillance at public hospitals.
analysis.event: The 2026 respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) season has ended, as reported by the National Institute for Communicable Diseases (NICD).
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The RSV season was marked by a moderate activity level, with the detection rate exceeding the seasonal threshold and being sustained for two consecutive weeks. Risk factors for severe disease include prematurity, congenital heart disease, and immunodeficiency.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Clinicians are advised to continue considering RSV in the differential diagnosis of respiratory illness, particularly in high-risk infants. Prevention measures remain important throughout the year, and additional RSV-specific preventive options are available for at-risk groups.

analysis.brief_en: The National Institute for Communicable Diseases (NICD) has announced the end of the 2026 respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) season, which began in week 11 (9 March 2026) and peaked in week 25 (15 June 2026). The season concluded in week 34 (17 August 2026), with RSV activity remaining moderate. The event was reported based on data from children aged <5 years in public hospitals participating in inpatient pneumonia surveillance. RSV is a significant cause of bronchiolitis and lower respiratory tract infections in young children, particularly infants, and can lead to severe illness in those with risk factors such as prematurity or immunodeficiency. Clinicians are urged to remain vigilant and consider RSV in the differential diagnosis of respiratory symptoms, especially in high-risk patients. Prevention measures, including avoiding close contact with sick individuals, regular handwashing, and covering coughs and sneezes, are emphasized. RSV-specific preventive options, such as palivizumab, are available for at-risk groups, though their high cost may limit use. The NICD also highlights the importance of general measures to reduce respiratory virus transmission year-round.
